teaser: In 1859, New Yorkers bought tickets and brought opera glasses to stare at one painting.
review_notes:
Admission 25 cents; about 12,000 visitors in roughly three weeks at the Tenth Street Studio Building, New York, spring 1859.
Sold to William T. Blodgett for $10,000, then the record for a living American artist.
Humboldt died 6 May 1859 before the painting could travel to Berlin.
Mark Twain (Samuel Clemens) letter to his brother Orion, 1860, after seeing it in St. Louis; I paraphrase rather than quote.
Church's signature is cut into the bark of the lit tree at lower left; not legible at this image size.
Size about 168 x 303 cm.
First public film screening counted as Paris, 1895 (Lumière).

lesson.text: You buy a ticket. You step into a darkened room, sit down on a bench with strangers, and face a glowing rectangle that shows a place you will never visit. That is a night at the movies. It is also what New Yorkers did in the spring of 1859, thirty-six years before the first public film screening, in front of this painting.

Frederic Church showed Heart of the Andes alone, in a studio building on Tenth Street. Entry cost 25 cents. He set the canvas in a massive dark wooden frame built like a window, with curtains drawn back at the sides. Gas lamps lit the picture and nothing else, and around it he arranged dried palm leaves brought home from South America.

Visitors were advised to bring opera glasses, the small binoculars used at the theater. People scanned the canvas inch by inch through them, or rolled a sheet of paper into a tube, so that each small circle looked like a separate real view.

Why would anyone need binoculars for a painting? Partly its size: about 1.7 meters high and 3 meters wide (5.5 by 10 feet). Mostly its density. Church painted a whole climb through the tropics, from steamy riverbank to permanent ice, and he kept every level sharp.

lesson.title: From ice to jungle
lesson.text: Travel the way the 1859 crowd did: top left first, then down through the climates.

spots.title: The white summit
spots.text: A snow dome modeled on Chimborazo, the giant volcano of Ecuador. It is the coldest place in the picture, and Church lets one clean patch of blue sky open right above it.

spots.title: The bare highlands
spots.text: Brown, treeless slopes fold across the middle. Thin air, cool nights, grass and rock. A wisp of smoke or mist rises from one ridge, the only movement up there.

spots.title: The settled plain
spots.text: Lower down the land turns green and flat. A cluster of pale buildings with a church sits beside still water: the mild zone, where people farm and build.

spots.title: The hot lowland
spots.text: A waterfall pours into a pool that catches the sunlight. Down here the air is warm and wet, and every bank is choked with growth.

lesson.text: Four climates in one frame: that idea came from a book. The German explorer Alexander von Humboldt had climbed in these mountains around 1800 and described how a tropical peak stacks the world's zones on top of each other. He also urged painters to go there and show it. Church took him at his word.

He went twice, in 1853 and in 1857, riding mules along Humboldt's old routes through Colombia and Ecuador and filling sketchbooks with plants, rocks and skies. Back in New York he assembled them. No single spot in the Andes looks like this. The painting is a composite, a view built from many real pieces.

Church hoped to ship the finished canvas to Berlin so that Humboldt, nearly 90, could see the land of his youth once more. Humboldt died in May 1859, while the painting was still drawing crowds in New York.

Church was a devout Protestant, and for him the exact study of nature and religious feeling belonged together. He placed a small scene of worship in this wilderness, easy to miss beside so much foliage.
Two tiny people have stopped to pray beside a path. Can you spot them and the thing they are praying to?

spots.title: The wayside cross
spots.text: A pale wooden cross stands where the sunlit path crests. One figure in red, with a companion, pauses in front of it. They are the only people shown up close, and they are about as big as a leaf.

lesson.text: Their smallness is the point. They give you the scale of everything else, and they tell you how to behave here: stop and look up. The lit path at their feet is also your way in. It starts at the bottom edge, where you stand, and leads the eye uphill toward the snow.
Church combined a scientist's precision with a preacher's sense of awe. Every plant is painted so a botanist could name it, and the whole is arranged to make you feel small.

How do you paint three meters of such detail without the picture falling apart? Church worked in oil with fine brushes over a careful drawing, finishing one area at a time. Then he tied it together with light: one beam enters from the left and strikes the path, the birch trunks and the falling water.

A young riverboat pilot named Samuel Clemens saw the picture on tour in St. Louis and wrote his brother that he had gone back more than once and still could not take it all in. The world would soon know him as Mark Twain.

The show ran about three weeks and drew around twelve thousand visitors. Then a collector paid $10,000 for the canvas, more than had ever been given for a work by a living American artist. Church was 33. The painting went on to London, where it was shown the same theatrical way.

The opera glasses did one more thing: they slowed people down. Nobody glanced and left. With the dark room gone, your own fingers can do that job. Wander the canvas at your own pace, corner by corner, the way the crowd of 1859 did.

spots.title: The signed tree
spots.text: A broken trunk catches the light at the left edge. Church cut his name and the date into its painted bark, as a traveler might carve a real tree. The letters are too fine to read at this size.

spots.title: White trunks
spots.text: Slender trees with pale, peeling bark rise against the dark slope. Their brightness pulls the right side forward, like actors stepping into a spotlight.

spots.title: Tree ferns
spots.text: Feathery fronds spread like umbrellas: ferns the size of small trees. To a New Yorker of 1859 they were as exotic as anything in a greenhouse.

spots.title: Blue blossoms
spots.text: A spray of pale blue flowers hangs in shade at the right edge. Church cools the corner with them, so the warm gold of the pool looks warmer.

spots.title: The pool
spots.text: Below the fall the water flattens and reflects the light, then breaks into white ripples. Look at how few strokes of white it takes to make it wet.

spots.title: Bare roots
spots.text: A mass of dark roots claws out over the bank where the soil has washed away. Decay and growth sit side by side all through this foreground.

spots.title: Cloud bank
spots.text: Gray and white clouds roll in over the far ranges. They flatten the top of the picture so that the one blue opening on the left, above the snow, feels like a window.

lesson.text: Today the canvas hangs in the Metropolitan Museum under even light, in a frame rebuilt to recall the lost original. Nobody charges you a quarter. But stand close, cup your hand into a tube and move it slowly across the surface, and you get a little of the 1859 show back.

quiz.question: How was Heart of the Andes first shown in 1859?
options: Free of charge in a public park
By itself, in a darkened room, for a 25-cent ticket
In a big group exhibition of American art
quiz.explanation: Church exhibited it alone with gaslight, curtains and a window-like frame, and charged 25 cents.

quiz.question: Whose writings sent Church to South America?
quiz.explanation: Humboldt had described the Andes and urged painters to go and paint them.

quiz.question: Is the view a single real place?
options: Yes, a valley near Quito painted on the spot
No, it was assembled in New York from many sketches
quiz.explanation: It is a composite built in the studio from two trips' worth of studies.

quiz.question: What are the two small figures on the path doing?
quiz.explanation: They have stopped before a wayside cross.

quiz.question: Why were visitors told to bring opera glasses?
options: To study the tiny details one patch at a time
Because the painting hung very high
To read the artist's printed guide
quiz.explanation: The canvas was so dense with detail that people explored it piece by piece.

quiz.question: What does the painting stack from top to bottom?
options: Climate zones, from ice down to hot lowland
quiz.explanation: It follows Humboldt's idea of a tropical mountain holding all climates at once.

facts.text: Humboldt traveled to New York to see the painting in 1859.
facts.explanation: He died in Berlin in May 1859 before the picture could be sent to him.

facts.text: The canvas sold for $10,000, a record at the time for a living American artist.
facts.explanation: A collector paid that sum right after the New York show.

facts.text: Church signed the picture by carving his name into a painted tree trunk.
facts.explanation: The signature is cut into the bark of the lit tree at lower left.
